$description: Tang Imperial (大唐) — the cosmopolitan grandeur of China's golden age, where Silk Road luxury met Confucian order

syncupsuite.foundation.story: The Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE) represents the apex of Chinese civilization — a cosmopolitan empire where Persian merchants, Buddhist monks, and Japanese scholars mingled in Chang'an, the world's largest city. Its palette comes from sancai (three-color) glazes, imperial silks dyed with mineral pigments, and the gilded bronzes of court ritual.
syncupsuite.foundation.philosophy: 大同 (Dàtóng) — Great Harmony through cosmopolitan confidence and ritual order

seedColors.name: Zhūshā Hóng (朱砂红)
seedColors.tradition: Cinnabar vermilion — the color of imperial seals, lacquerware, and temple gates. Ground from mercury sulfide ore, it was the most valued pigment in East Asia.
seedColors.source: Chinese Pigments: A Technical Study, Rutherford J. Gettens

seedColors.name: Jīn Sè (金色)
seedColors.tradition: Imperial gold — from gilt bronze ritual vessels (鎏金) and the golden reliquaries of Famen Temple. Symbolizes prosperity and the mandate of heaven.
seedColors.source: The Golden Age of Chinese Art: The Lively Tang Dynasty, Maxwell Hearn

seedColors.name: Cuì Lǜ (翠绿)
seedColors.tradition: Jade green — the color of nephrite and jadeite prized above gold. Tang celadon glazes approached this color through iron-reduction firing.
seedColors.source: Chinese Jade: From the Neolithic to the Qing, Jessica Rawson

seedColors.name: Mò Hēi (墨黑)
seedColors.tradition: Ink black — from pine soot ink sticks used in Tang calligraphy. The foundation of Chinese writing from Yan Zhenqing's regular script.
seedColors.source: A History of Chinese Calligraphy, Yuho Tseng

seedColors.name: Xuān Zhǐ (宣紙)
seedColors.tradition: Xuan paper — the absorbent mulberry-bark paper from Anhui province, unchanged since the Tang. Its warm tone defines Chinese painting ground.
seedColors.source: Paper and Printing (Science and Civilisation in China), Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin

seedColors.name: Zǐ Tán (紫檀)
seedColors.tradition: Rosewood purple — from the prized zitan hardwood of imperial furniture. The deepest, most restrained luxury of the Tang court.
seedColors.source: Chinese Furniture: A Guide to Collecting Antiques, Karen Mazurkewich
